title: Wine Grapes Are Thriving In One of the Driest Places On Earth
summary:
Over the last two decades, winemakers have been flocking to Chile’s Atacama Desert for its distinct and vibrant character.

The post Wine Grapes Are Thriving In One of the Driest Places On Earth appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
When you step off the plane in Copiapó, the gateway to Chile‘s Atacama region, the vast, dusty landscape makes you wonder how a single vine could survive here—let alone thrive. 

The answer lies in the transverse valleys that stretch from the Andes Mountains to the Pacific Ocean, flourishing even alongside and within the Atacama, the world’s driest non-polar desert. Cooling coastal breezes, rivers, and temperature shifts at higher altitudes make viticulture possible in this seemingly inhospitable landscape. 

Since the 16th century, locals in the northern Huasco, Elqui, and Limarí Valleys have cultivated grapes primarily for Pisco. Over the last two decades, however, wine producers have begun exploring this area, known as Norte Verde (which translates to Green North).

Wines made here are vibrant and fresh, with a distinct character that sets them apart from those of Chile’s central valleys. This isn’t a passing trend but an emerging expression of Chilean wine built on a shared commitment to premium, low-intervention, terroir-driven winemaking.

Huasco Valley: Freshness in the Atacama Desert

In 2010, Ventisquero Wine Estates planted its first vines in the Huasco Valley, a remote region on the southern border of the Atacama Desert where few producers had previously ventured. 

“Even there, in the driest desert on earth, the Pacific Ocean and the Camanchaca fog bring freshness and balance to the vineyards,” says Horacio Fuentes, Ventisquero’s export director.

The estate’s vines grow just 13 miles from the coast, and despite its location, the valley is not hot. Thanks to the sea, average annual temperatures range from 62°F to 66°F, and the Huasco River ensures water is readily available, too.

The range of soils includes sandy loam and clay with varying salt content, but it’s the limestone that defines the valley’s character.

“What surprises people most about these wines is not their power, but their elegance and freshness,” Fuentes says. “You get purity, tension, minerality, and natural acidity.” 

Ventisquero’s goal is to make wine that reflects its origin. Winemakers achieve that end with a low-intervention approach, employing native yeast and aging in untoasted foudres or cement eggs, and avoiding filtering before bottling.

The Elqui Valley: Vineyards that Scrape the Stars

At the edge of the Atacama Desert, the picturesque Elqui Valley is renowned for its Pisco production. But it’s also an emerging region for delicious wines with dramatic tension.

Agriculture in Elqui follows the Turbio River from the Andes Mountains to the Pacific Ocean. Wine producers tend to prefer higher elevation areas of over 7,000 feet, where the vines grow on granite, clay, and silt soils, and diurnal temperature shifts caused by high altitude and clear skies allow the grapes to fully mature.

“Making mountain wine limits you in many ways, but the grape quality is unique,” says Viñedos de Alcohuaz winemaker Rosario Fillol. “You get intense concentration, excellent natural acidity, and vibrancy.” Here, winemakers celebrate the incredibly distinct landscape, and are genuinely committed to terroir and a clear regional identity.

“Producers in the Norte Verde respect the land and work with less conventional winemaking approaches that reflect the region in the glass,” adds Fillol. 

Her team stomps grapes barefoot in granite lagares made from mountain rocks, seeking a softer extraction for an enhanced tannic structure. They also utilize concrete eggs and amphorae to allow micro-oxygenation without imparting flavors, so the Elqui character shines through.

Limarí Valley: The Power of Limestone and Ocean Influence

The Limarí valley is in the Coquimbo region next to the Atacama, and its top vineyards are located near the Pacific Ocean. This coastal influence lowers temperatures, reduces sunlight, and brings morning fog and higher humidity. As a result, grapes here ripen slowly, which is crucial for delicate varieties like Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

But growing vines in Limarí is not easy. In some areas, that coastal influence can complicate things, leaving plants needing protection from the strong ocean breezes, and producers like Tabali having to blend aquifer water with river water to reduce salinity before irrigating.

Chardonnay, in particular, greatly benefits from Limarí’s terroir. Utilizing the region’s limestone soils, which provide wines with exquisite vibrancy, winemakers can maximize the grape’s unique flavor profile.

“Limarí Chardonnay tends to show a more restrained aromatic profile, less intense and less fruity, with a distinct flavor expression,” says Felipe Müller, CEO and chief winemaker at Tabali. The wines are “sometimes slightly saline, with a chemical balance that sets it apart from other cool-climate regions in Chile.” 

Seeing the success of Limarí’s wines, powerhouse labels like Santa Rita and Amelia (Concha y Toro) have started to source grapes and produce wines in the region. These bottlings can be bright and flinty or focused and elegant, but all express the Valley’s signature mineral characteristics.

Additionally, a growing focus on premium wines has been key in establishing the northern valleys as a quality wine region.

“There are few wineries in this area, and the overall quality level is significantly higher compared to the Central Valley and other regions with many producers,” says Müller. “This has been crucial in quickly establishing many of these wines among Chile’s top offerings.” 

In a relatively short time, wines from Huasco, Elqui, and Limarí have developed strong identities that express and surpass the extreme climate where the vines grow. Winemaking in Chile has never been easy—but it’s never been more exciting, either.

title: Why ‘Quality Over Quantity’ Is Good for the Wine Industry
summary:
Consumption may be down, but open-mindedness and willingness to spend is up.

The post Why ‘Quality Over Quantity’ Is Good for the Wine Industry appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Chris Liu believes that there’s a bright side to shorter bar tabs. 

“People are drinking less in terms of quantity, but I find them more discerning in terms of quality,” says the beverage director of Bloomsday, a wine bar and restaurant in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. “They’re very intentional about what they buy.”

The practice extends beyond Bloomsday’s barstools. People of all ages, appetites, and tax brackets are recalibrating their consumption habits and redefining value at the bar and bottle shop—and it could have a big impact on wine. Whether that’s a positive development depends on your outlook and how much time we all have. 

As countless headlines and Reddit threads will tell you, modern wine businesses face an array of evolving social, economic, and environmental challenges. But the drink-less-but-better movement isn’t an existential threat. It’s proof that many people who are cutting back are still interested in wine and eager to make the most out of every glass or bottle they try. 

Armchair analysts who bemoan generational shifts and elegize consumption data tend to ignore this crucial detail: People who are drinking wine are doing so more skillfully and thoughtfully than ever before. That’s not a silver lining so much as lightning in a bottle. The only question is whether there’s enough time for it to ignite.

Curiosity Takes Center Stage

“There’s been a steady evolution in the way people drink wine,” says Jamie Ritchie, the managing director of international auctions at Berry Bros. & Rudd in Washington, D.C. In previous decades, many collectors would purchase multiple cases from known regions or producers without investigating their preferences or looking beyond the usual suspects. 

These days, “people are more curious and willing to experiment,” he says. “The curiosity goes across generations. There’s a gravitation at all levels and at all ages for people to understand a bit about what they’re drinking and get excited about different things.” 

Chase Sinzer agrees. The owner of Claud, Stars, and Penny in New York City has observed a sea change in the ways people approach wine lists. In the 2010s, guests at restaurants where he worked would come in and say, “‘I know what I want, and it’s going to be Bordeaux or Brunello, and I’d like to spend this amount of money, and I don’t want anyone to talk to me,’” he recalls. “That same person now goes, ‘Can you please give me a few options? I can’t wait to hear what you have to say.’”

Ritchie links some of the open-mindedness and exploratory zeal to the effects of the pandemic. During shutdowns, many people studied wine. When hospitality businesses reopened, they shed their sweatpants, went out to bars and restaurants, and were eager to taste everything that the wide world of wine had to offer. Like their customers, retailers experienced these discovery trends, too.

Better, Not More

This same time period coincided with an enduring emphasis on moderation over excess. “Everyone is drinking less, for health reasons or generally for interest in living a more balanced life,” says Ritchie. 

That’s not a death knell, either. It’s a call to action. When someone is more knowledgeable and curious about what they drink, they can investigate each purchase to tailor it to their tastes and budgets. These are prime conditions to create lasting relationships with wine—ones with more long-term benefits than intermittent, happy-hour binges.

This all presents an opportunity for sommeliers, salespeople, and other wine professionals to meet people where they are and cultivate their curiosity. It’s a chance to learn from and avoid the knee-jerk anti-Merlot or Anything But Chardonnay sentiments of previous eras that led many folks to write off entire categories or wine itself without a second thought (or glass). “We’re making up for previous sins of sommeliers of different generations now,” Sinzer says.  

Besides, in the current economic moment, few of us are sitting on mountains of surplus cash to throw at lackluster wine. Trading multiple mediocre glasses for something you really love aligns with the way many people spend. They might be willing to shell out a few extra dollars for one great glass or bottle from a producer who shares their values, if consumer behaviors in fair-trade coffee, organic produce, and thrifted versus fast fashion are any indication.  

A quality-over-quantity mindset creates new and better points of access to wine, Liu says. “People are willing to spend $15 on something good and only have one bottle that night, rather than spend $15 on a case of poorly made beverages without thinking about it,” he says. “That’s actually helping the industry in a lot of ways because you have a new entry to the market that’s not garbage.”

Meaningful change takes time, and many grape growers, winemakers, and retailers need the market to rebound yesterday. But wine is a long game, too. After 8,000 years, how we think about, make, and drink it continues to evolve. Even if you only have one pour on any given night, that glass is still half-full.

title: Why ABV Is Showing Up on Cocktail Menus
summary:
These days, drinkers can cut back on their alcohol intake with increasing precision.

The post Why ABV Is Showing Up on Cocktail Menus appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • American alcohol consumption is at a record low, which is driving a rise in low-proof options.
  • Some bars now list abv on menus to help consumers decide what to order.
  • Transparency in drink strength improves hospitality, promotes inclusion, and helps businesses sell more lower-abv beverages.

As evidenced by our current era of mini martinis and tiny cocktails, zero-proof drinks, and low-proof spirits, the trend persists: Everyone is drinking less. 

A 2026 Gallup poll reports that though the share of Americans who say they drink alcohol is at 54%—a record low for this annual survey that has been conducted since the end of Prohibition.  More and more people are exploring non-alcoholic options or simply reducing the number of glasses they have with dinner. These days, drinkers can even cut back on their alcohol intake with increasing precision.

In the same way that nutritional data like calories and grams of protein started appearing on menus, a growing number of cocktail lists around the country are displaying a drink’s abv (alcohol by volume). The trend allows bartenders and owners to give their cocktails—and alcohol levels—deeper levels of consideration and intention at all stages, from recipe development to marketing.

A Tool for Discovery

According to Kraig Rovensky, partner and beverage director at Life on Mars in Seattle, local drinkers are already accustomed to seeing abv info on menus because of craft beer culture. At Life on Mars in Seattle, the espresso martini is listed at 20% abv, while the Pathfinder Spritz is at just 0.03%. Since the bar’s opening in 2019, the menu has always listed each item’s abv, Rovensky says, because he wants guests to feel confident about what they order and not worry about mistakenly getting something that’s too strong for them. 

“Most people don’t know how different the alcohol content is in vermouth versus whiskey,” Rovensky says. “I’ve heard from people they were shocked at how much alcohol was in an Old Fashioned versus a spritz. As beverage professionals, this is obvious to us, but I think we forget just how little the general consumer knows.” 

Stuart Jensen, owner of Peach Crease Club in Denver, believes that offering abv information to guests is a natural extension of hospitality. It’s a way to guide and educate guests, empowering them with the intel they need to become savvy bargoers each time they order a Guinness (4.2% abv) or an Old Fashioned (44.9% abv). 

“It’s not something that everyone notices or takes into consideration, but those that do are very appreciative,” Jensen says. “And the staff is happy to have one more tool that helps them point guests in the direction of a drink they’ll enjoy.” Declaring abv percentages also helps bar teams educate customers unfamiliar with rare or unusual spirits and drinks. The Hellenic restaurant MEZŌ Mediterranean in Dedham, Massachusetts, serves Greek beers like Fix Hellas and Mythos and traditional spirits like ouzo and tsipouro, with which guests may be unfamiliar. 

Co-owner and executive chef George Panagopoulos says that adding abv information to MEZŌ’s menu has given diners another point of reference. “It helps set expectations and makes people feel more confident trying something new,” he says. “Guests appreciate the transparency and the information often sparks conversations with our team about Greek drinking culture and the stories behind these beverages.” 

Louis Lin, the chef and owner of Xiao Ye in Portland, Oregon, was thinking about both approachability and the bottom line of his business when considering adding the abv info to his drink menu. His wife and business partner, Jolyn Chen, is not a big drinker, he says: “She’s always been really aware of whether wine lists and cocktail menus feel approachable to someone who doesn’t drink.” And so he began to view the practice of listing abv percentages, whether for his gin-based Italo Disco at 27% or the Pandan Coconut Sparkler at 0%, as an invitation to those who don’t drink or drink less to find something they might enjoy. Moreover, it helps the business’ bottom line. 

“If a diner gets stuck with a super-boozy drink they can’t finish, there’s a chance they won’t order another,” Lin says. “But if they end up drinking and loving something that’s 12%, maybe they’ll be inclined to get another knowing that they won’t overdo it.”

Mixing and Matching on the Menu

At the buzzy new restaurant Oriana in New York City’s Nolita neighborhood, zero-abv cocktails are listed alongside the rest of the main menu. The non-alcoholic Ghost Flame with black tea, pepper, and NA amaro sits right next to the mezcal-centric Smoking Sol with an abv of 20%, rather than being relegated to a separate, perhaps less-loved section. 

“We put just as much thought and development into those drinks,” says Oriana’s owner and sommelier Cedric Nicaise. This subtle difference makes the low- and no-abv offerings feel just as intentional and significant as every other cocktail they serve, he explains, and guests “appreciate having that information available and the way it’s presented.”

As a trend, listing the alcohol content on menus is likely to stick around. As a statement on how we drink and dine today, it’s all quite fitting. Much like how these low- or no-abv tipples are just as well crafted as spirit-forward heavy hitters on menus, drinking less or not drinking alcohol is just as valid a vibe as tossing back martinis with urbane swagger. As ever, information is power and gestures of inclusion are meaningful—in both life and cocktail menus.

title: These Wineries Are Just as Serious About ‘Merroir’ as They Are Terroir
summary:
In places like the Chesapeake Bay, winemakers and seafood purveyors are bridging the gap between land and water in pursuit of a common goal.

The post These Wineries Are Just as Serious About ‘Merroir’ as They Are Terroir appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
On a cool November evening on Virginia’s Eastern shore in the Chesapeake Bay, a small but bustling crowd gathers around wine and oysters.

Tables are topped with plates of the freshly shucked bivalves, and each adult sips a glass of wine. The scene, framed by the Bay glittering in the background and rows of trellised grapevines rustling in the wind, depicts a typical weekend at the Chatham Vineyards tasting room from November to March. The collaborative event, called “Winter Wine and Oyster Weekend,” is the perfect showcase of “merroir.” 

Coined in the early 2000s, the term “merroir” is the water version of terroir: it refers to when surrounding marine elements impact the flavor profile of marine life. Just as wine has terroir, oysters have merroir. And in places like the Chesapeake Bay, the largest United States estuary (a mostly encapsulated large body of water in which fresh water meets seawater), winemakers and seafood purveyors are bridging the gap between land and water in pursuit of a common goal: building a more sustainable environment while nurturing the local economy.

What Goes Better Than Wine and Oysters?

From a flavor perspective, oysters and wine make natural companions.

Chatham Vineyards, whose vines are just 300 yards away from the oyster beds, has been hosting its wine and oyster pairing events for 17 years. The winery’s steel-fermented, minimal intervention Chardonnay, one of its most successful bottlings, is a stalwart in its consistency of product and ability to pair with Chesapeake Bay oysters.

“There is a unique minerality in the wine that counters the salinity of Chesapeake Bay oysters, while a ripe fruit component matches the sweetness of the oyster,” says John Wehner, Chatham Winery’s owner.

About 15 miles north of Chatham Winery lies Laughing King Oyster Company and Vessel Farm Winery. Owners Thomas and Erin Haney founded the oyster company first and then established the vineyard less than a mile from the oyster beds, with the intent of pairing the wine with the oysters. As Thomas puts it, “the focus is small-batch production with high quality” that offers a full spectrum of the Eastern Shore flavor profiles, like salinity, umami, and minerality. 

While over 50 grapes were initially planted in the vineyards, Vermentino is emerging as the highlighted wine for the oyster pairing, which “has been a way to introduce a grape most people are not familiar with,” says Thomas.

The Dog and Oyster Micro Vineyard, located further north, has hosted wine and seafood events for 15 years. Like Chatham Winery, they offer a Chardonnay that is fermented in stainless steel to preserve the freshness and minerality to pair with the oysters.

Protecting the Bay with Merroir and Terroir

Aquaculture and oyster farms are vital to the Chesapeake Bay estuary. Estuaries are known for their brackish water—the mix of fresh and saltwater—that nurtures the ideal environment for organisms like oysters to grow. That set of conditions is mutually beneficial: a full-term oyster is capable of cleaning 50 gallons of water a day. The mollusks also lower the carbon footprint by utilizing carbon in the formation of their shells, and they further aid in lowering oxygen depletion by consuming algae, thus minimizing dead zones in the water.

In terms of flavor, bodies of water like the Chesapeake Bay promote the balance of saltiness (from the seawater) and sweetness (from the silt bottom and fresh water) that makes oysters delicious. It is only fitting that a region that is ramping up its wine production fosters a union with a product unique to this environment.

While there are some 250 commercial aquaculture enterprises in the Chesapeake Bay, many of the wineries are not part of an established wine trail. These unique “merroir/terroir” experiences in this region invite and inform a sustainable path forward for both wine and oysters.

title: Southeastern IPA Is Coming for New England and the West Coast
summary:
These refreshing citrus-forward brews are exactly what you want to sip on a hot summer's day.

The post Southeastern IPA Is Coming for New England and the West Coast appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
If you’re in the Southeastern United States right now, we don’t have to tell you that it’s hot and humid. In the area from the Carolinas through Georgia and Northern Alabama, we’re talking highs in the 90s with dew points hovering in the mid-70s. As a result, more often than not, beer drinkers reach for something light, refreshing, and repeatable.

However, the long months of heat and humidity present a unique conundrum to Southeastern beermakers: how to find the creative sweet spot between what is refreshing and what provides a more robust beer drinking experience.

Enter the Southeastern IPA, a style that is beginning to take hold in the region.

“It just makes sense,” says Blake Tyers, co-founder of Creature Comforts Brewing Co. in Athens, GA. “There is just a regionality to how people approach beer.” 

In the American Southeast, that equates to a lighter and leaner IPA with citrus flavors. So, what is a Southeastern IPA? Proponents say it’s as much about what it isn’t as what it is: not too bitter, not too high-alcohol, and not too heavy or sweet. 

In the mid 2010s, when Tyers and the Creatures Comfort team set out to create Tropicalia, one of the company’s flagship beers, they had internal discussions about what might constitute “Southeastern IPA” characteristics without outwardly calling it as such. It was simply something they were making for IPA drinkers living in the Southeast.

The same was true when brewers at Edmund’s Oast Brewing Co. in Charleston, South Carolina, created their flagship beer, Bound by Time. “It’s hot and humid here for a long time, so the style of IPAs that we want to drink in that weather is light and lean and really refreshing,” says co-founder and partner Scott Shor. “Bound By Time fits that. It’s still hop-forward, still IPA, but not with a cloying, sweet finish.” 

After Tyers and Shor connected over the beer moniker while at a beer dinner in Decatur, GA, this spring, they decided to collaborate on a Southeastern IPA that was announced as such on the can. Spatial Distortion is the result, brewed with Amarillo Cryo, Simcoe Hyperboost, and Citra hops. It has 6.5% abv and a firm 45 IBUs with just a touch of haze. 

Meanwhile, up in Charlotte, North Carolina, Chad Henderson, head brewer and co-owner of NoDa Brewing Company, has been creating in the same vein. “We love IPAs but something with too-high alcohol hits too fast in this heat,” he says. “Then again, session beers don’t always fit the bill, either.” 

Characteristics of a Southeastern IPA

  • Aromatic and hop-forward
  • Leaner, rounder, and softer, and with less malt than an English IPA
  • A dry finish supported by yeast strains
  • 5-7 % abv for drinkability
  • Dry-hopped

Henderson’s brewery has been experimenting with a lighter Southeastern IPA style as well, morphing it through a few iterations before landing on True Grit, a beer with 5.5% abv. It’s brewed with grits to add a clean, crisp finish to complement the intensity of the Simcoe, Mosaic, Citra, Centennial, and Chinook hops. Currently sold out, it was one of Henderson’s favorite brews to date. 

“So clean and refreshing, it really got at what we were going for,” he says. “I’m very proud of that beer. With the amount of hops in it, it’s very expensive to make, though.”

Comeback Sauce, the second Southeastern IPA collaboration from Edmund’s and Creature Comforts, debuted in early 2026. Named for the Mississippi-born dipping sauce and salad dressing, the beer is proudly rooted in its region. “It’s not West coast; it’s not New England,” the packaging proclaims. “It’s a Southern thing.”

title: Moldovan Wine Is Taking on the World
summary:
After losing support from Russia, Moldova shifted its focus from sweet, bulk wines to higher-quality bottlings with global appeal.

The post Moldovan Wine Is Taking on the World appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Despite political instability and poverty, wine remains central to Moldova’s identity, economy, and national recovery.
  • Russian export bans forced Moldovan wineries to modernize production and adopt higher international quality standards.
  • Moldova now successfully exports higher-value, quality wines globally, shifting its market focus toward Western countries.

That the small former Soviet republic of Moldova remains one of Europe’s poorest countries is perhaps unsurprising. It is perched right on the geographical edge of NATO, borders Europe’s largest armed conflict since WWII, and is home to the breakaway republic of Transnistria, widely regarded as a de facto Russian puppet state. Yet, despite such an uncomfortable geopolitical reality, Moldova is gradually finding its footing, and wine is leading its transformation. 

Winemaking is deeply intertwined with Moldovan identity, having played a central role in the region’s life for centuries. During the Soviet period, Moldova was the Union’s largest wine supplier (estimates suggest it was responsible for every second bottle consumed in the USSR) and today, the industry remains central to its economy. 

In fact, for a country with a population of over two million, wine directly employs around 150,000 people, and exports alone account for approximately 3% of national GDP. Ștefan Iamandi, director of Moldova’s National Office of Vine and Wine (ONVV), points out that “if we include all the supporting industries like glass bottle manufacturing and wine tourism, you could easily double that figure.”

First Steps Towards Modernity

Its role as the Soviet Union’s principal wine supplier sustained Moldova’s economy in the years following independence, when Russia remained its main export market. But that dependence also left the country acutely vulnerable to political and cultural influence from Moscow. That reality became starkly apparent in 2006, when Russia responded to Moldova’s increasingly westward orientation by imposing the first in a series of punitive embargoes. 

“They dealt a serious blow to our wine sector, but they also pushed us to seek out new markets,” says Inga Manuilenco, enologist at Kazayak Vin and Suvorov-Vin. “To meet international quality standards, we realized that we needed to fundamentally overhaul the entire industry.”

Wineries began upgrading vineyards, equipment, and production processes through both public and private support, including international assistance programs such as USAID. They also considered Western tastes, gradually moving away from the sweeter, fruit-forward wines favored by Russian drinkers and, at the same time, shifting from the Aligotés and Rkatsitelis of Soviet times toward grape varieties with more widespread appeal.

“In the past, we often focused on internationally renowned varieties,” says Manuilenco. “Now, more and more attention is being paid to indigenous and regional varieties such as Viorica, Riton, and Floricica,” which, in Iamandi’s estimation, already account for almost a third of all plantings, and continue to expand.

Back to the Drawing Board

Recognizing the pivotal role wine would play in the country’s future prosperity, the government stepped in to help, launching Moldova Wine Day. The event has become a key platform for promoting Moldovan wine and a significant source of revenue for the country as a whole, too. “We have held it each year on the first weekend of October since 2002,” Iamandi explains. “Last year, we had around 150,000 attendees, including 20,000 tourists, which for Moldova is a huge number, especially when concentrated into just three days.”

In addition, the government enacted a series of legislative reforms and, in an effort to gradually increase the country’s visibility and support the industry’s development, established the ONVV, along with its public-facing brand Wine of Moldova, in 2013. Recent initiatives reflect the country’s rapidly growing confidence and ambition, from hosting the sparkling edition of the prestigious Concours Mondial de Bruxelles wine competition to welcoming the 2025 World Congress of Vine and Wine, one of the industry’s leading global gatherings.

Success Through Struggle

Plenty of challenges lay ahead of course, but Moldova’s wine industry is clear-eyed and steadfast. The country is still largely perceived as a producer of cheap, bulk plonk, and that’s assuming people even know of its existence. Not to mention the added weight of its ongoing geopolitical dilemma. “Even if Moldova remains stable, the mere fact that it is located near a zone of military conflict can increase the perception of risk,” Manuilenco admits. “This affects the cost of capital, the speed of investment decision-making, and companies’ willingness to invest in long-term projects.” 

Despite these obstacles, the progress of Moldova’s wine—and its positive impact on the country as a whole—is tangible. Today, 35 years after the collapse of the Soviet Bloc, nearly 70% of Moldovan wine exports go to Europe and America, with another roughly 10% destined for Asia and Africa (with Nigeria an increasingly enthusiastic buyer).

“In March 2013, I organised the launch of the Wine of Moldova brand at ProWein,” recalls Thomas Brandl, a marketing professional who has worked with Moldovan wine for several years. “Despite our best efforts to promote the presentation, barely a dozen journalists and trade representatives attended, and the quality of the wines was so-so. Back at Prowein ten years later, I had a full house, and the best red wine at the Concours Mondial de Bruxelles came from Moldova.”

Recent data confirms that Moldova’s wine sector is indeed moving upmarket. Over the past decade, export volumes have declined by 11% but value has risen by 23%, indicating that the country is steadily shifting away from the gargantuan output of the Soviet era and establishing itself as a producer of quality liquid. There might still be challenges ahead, but Moldova is steadily emerging from its troubled past, the success of its wine propelling it toward a more prosperous future.

title: Will Home Wine Rooms Replace the Cellar?
summary:
Wine rooms offer flexibility, show-stopping bottle display, and endless  opportunities for entertaining.

The post Will Home Wine Rooms Replace the Cellar? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Among the luxurious perks of residing at 53 West 53, the sculptural Midtown Manhattan tower brought to life by architect Jean Nouvel and the late interior designer Thierry Despont, is access to its temperature-controlled wine room and vault. 

Crowned with an octagonal double-height gold-leaf ceiling, the lavish tasting area is adorned with walnut and cork flooring and leather and metallic accents. Like a members-only club, it’s a place for residents to unwind and converse over bottles curated by the in-house sommelier for tastings and small group dinners, while serving as a secure storage facility for their own beloved stashes. But these social amenity spaces aren’t relegated to swank condominium communities; increasingly, they are becoming dynamic, well-designed additions to private homes.

“It’s not just about racking wine anymore—people want to make sure the space is showstopping,” says Jerry Garcia, custom wine cellar specialist at Wine Enthusiast. “In the last couple of months, I’ve seen an increase in customers who want to mix their wine cellar with a bar and custom cabinetry. It’s a move toward luxury and a custom feeling.”

A Flexible Alternative to the Wine Cellar

Over the past several years, David Ries, principal of New York-based design studio Ries Hayes, has seen a deluge of client requests for spaces that “work harder and serve multiple purposes,” as he puts it. 

The wine room is no exception. “A traditional wine cellar is fairly locked into a single function, but moving the wine into display refrigeration allows the collection to become part of almost any room.”

For a Long Island residence in Water Mill, for example, Ries Hayes flanked a bar with imposing glass-and-steel wine refrigerators that serve as practical yet visually arresting storage units. They also organically forge a hangout space for watching television or enjoying a meal amid orderly rows of bottles. “Because it opens directly to the larger living room, it feels less like a separate, specialized room and more like an extension of how the house is actually lived in,” Ries explains.

Located on the lower level of a beach house, the wine room subtly references its East End surroundings with a cool, sophisticated palette of driftwood-toned stained oak, quartz floor tiles, and charcoal quartzite countertops buoyed by integrated lighting. In Ries’ eyes, “Layering in light at low, mid, and high levels makes the room visually dramatic and playful.” 

Putting Wine Front and Center

Paul Kropp, co-founder and COO of the Michigan-based cabinet maker Bakes & Kropp, remembers when home entertaining was dominated by spiffed-up basements. The wine cellar, then, typically the domain of subterranean spaces, came in handy for replenishing bottles on demand. Now, hosts and oenophiles are eager to illuminate everyday living spaces with the wines they’ve amassed, as they would heirlooms lining a mantelpiece.

“Wine is not only a part of fine dining, but a symbol of the good life. Passionate wine collectors want to live in a space where they can see their collection,” explains Kropp. “They’re proud of it, they’ve likely spent decades working on it, and they want to show it off.” 

Consider the homeowners in coastal Michigan who had a specific directive for Bakes & Kropp: a refrigerated room that could hold 350 bottles alongside a back bar for entertaining by their boat. Working with local firm Chatham House Interiors, Bakes & Kropp translated that objective into a bespoke space that highlights functionality. The array of wines is almost magnified behind glass, pragmatically nestled between dark truffle-hued cabinets incorporating intricate metalwork on the doors, a quartzite backsplash and countertops, and convenient prep and storage areas. 

To ensure a wine room seamlessly blends into a living area, Kropp advises designing the storage portion “as a shallow space that extends along the length of the wall,” showcasing the bottles being stored. “That way, it serves more as a piece of artwork at the end of a room,” he says.” Even the labels are artwork,” he elaborates.

The Chic Way to Entertain

Whiling away an entire evening in a cramped living room or formal dining room can become monotonous. For homeowners who want to punctuate their soirées with a proper wine tasting, a striking room dedicated to pouring and sipping is a surefire way to surprise and beguile their guests. 

“A cellar can feel like storage, but a wine room feels like an experience. People want a space that’s about the ritual of choosing a bottle,” says Jennifer Miller, founder of her eponymous Los Angeles design studio.

In a Montecito, California, residence Miller worked on, the wine room sits just off the dining room. “We chose a steel-and-glass door so that even when it’s closed, you still catch a glimpse of the walnut paneling and the glow of the interior lighting,” she says. 

And while it flows naturally into the dining room, the space intentionally shines on its own, enveloped in rich millwork paired with muted tones. “The light fixture is a standout. It’s almost like the jewelry of the room, which is exactly the effect we’re always chasing with lighting,” Miller explains. “Positioned right over the tasting counter, it creates this warm pool of light that draws you to the center of the room.” 

Certainly, it’s an inviting, personalized contrast to the dark cellar tucked away below ground. “If someone is into wine they want to show off their collection and incorporate it into gatherings with family friends, where they can see the wine cellar,” Garcia adds. “They want to make it the talk of the day.”

title: 8 Dreamy Home Wine Cellars You’ll Wish Were Yours
summary:
Jaw-dropping wine cellars aren’t just for restaurants. These home cellars prove it.

The post 8 Dreamy Home Wine Cellars You’ll Wish Were Yours appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Long gone are the days of musty, no-frills wine cellars. Creating the proper environment for aging and storage, of course, remains the priority for these utilitarian spaces. But a lot of time and money can go into cultivating a wine collection, so many design-savvy oenophiles opt to show off their treasures in stylish layouts. Whether it weaves in striking lighting, vintage finds, or made-to-order furniture, the contemporary wine cellar is now regarded as yet another room to gather and celebrate. Here are eight eye-catching examples.

An Intimate Tasting Space with Polish

Hillsborough, California

Only four leather chairs surround the marble tasting table anchoring the wine cellar Heather Hilliard brought to life for a private California residence. She wanted to create an intimate, comfortable space for the clients to enjoy wine tastings with a small group of guests, but with “the polished atmosphere and sense of experience you might find in a favorite restaurant,” explains the San Francisco-based designer. It’s joined by stone flooring that grounds the cellar and glass walls that ensure it’s visually open. “The cellar accommodates approximately 1,000 bottles stored horizontally on lit shelves so the collection becomes part of the architecture while remaining easy to view and access,” adds Hilliard.

A Cinematic Cellar Starring Prized Bottles

Greenwich, Connecticut

Since her clients are avid wine collectors, Taylor Lagerloef, founder and principal designer of Studio Lagerloef in New York, designed a cinematic cellar in a Greenwich, Connecticut, home—in collaboration with Cardello Architects and builder Hobbs, Inc.—to showcase an impressive stash. “They didn’t want the collection hidden away; they wanted to live with it,” Lagerloef points out. Along one wall, Lagerloef and her team built open shelving to highlight large-format bottles, favorite labels, and wine crates, and the backlit stone wall further amplifies the display. “The lighting turns rows of bottles into something that feels almost sculptural, and because the room is glass-enclosed and visible from the living space, the collection becomes part of the home’s everyday narrative,” she says. Polished concrete flooring and VeroMetal soffits add intriguing contrast to the wood-paneled ceiling and framed vintage wine map.

A Clandestine Mountainside Cave

Teton Village, Wyoming

Underneath a nearly 10,000-square-foot ski-in/ski-out, stone-and-timber house in Teton Village, Wyoming, CLB Architects dug a well below the lowest footings. Here, the wine cellar, part of an addition, is a departure from the existing dwelling’s traditional mountain architecture. A blackened steel handrail leads down to a massive area capable of holding 7,500 bottles. “The vision was to create a wine cellar that felt like a secret cave carved from solid stone,” says Montana-based CLB Architects principal Sam Ankeny. To enhance the carved effect on the walls, a split-face, natural cleft is mixed with honed Valser Quartz, while the ceiling is lined with subtle barrel-vaulted mahogany on the ceiling to add “warmth and evoke the sensation of being inside a wine barrel,” Ankeny adds. One exterior wall of the chic, subterranean grotto is outfitted with a thin-profile sliding glass system to capture natural light and seamlessly connect to the Rocky Mountain landscape.

A Resort-Like Wine Escape in the Hills

Beverly Hills, California

Boutique hotels were the inspiration for this narrow, four-story abode set high atop a ridge in Beverly Hills. “Solving the long, skinny site problem created an opportunity for many levels and spaces,” says Marc Whipple, founder of Whipple Russell Architects. This includes an entertainment hub including a poker room, theater, and a hybrid wine cellar and custom humidor that the Sherman Oaks-based architecture firm hatched in partnership with Troy Adams Design. Floor-to-ceiling dark-tinted glass reveals illuminated bottle storage that meshes with bespoke furniture, a marble wet bar, Spanish cedar, and Henge lighting. Fresh air and gorgeous views await right outside on the adjacent covered terrace, complete with a cozy fire feature that’s a prime spot to enjoy a glass on a chilly evening.

A Euro-Inspired Shrine to Red Wine

Kleinburg, Ontario

Jessica Neilas, founder and creative director of Toronto-based Wolfe Interior Design, envisioned this cellar in an Ontario home as a place to settle in around the table in the center. ”Somewhere that could accommodate both a quiet glass of wine and a night of revelry,” as she puts it. The client’s passion for red wine translated to deep red marble and burgundy leather paired with aged brass tones. But the most dramatic element is the arched wood-and-glass enclosure. “There is a deliberate transition from the brighter architecture outside into something darker, warmer, and more intimate,” says Neilas. “It feels almost like looking into a tiny European bar or enoteca—a little hidden room where you expect to find great wine, music, conversation, and people lingering much longer than they intended.”

Climate-Controlled Centerpiece with a Luxe Touch

Atlanta, Georgia

The terrace level of an Atlanta townhouse beckons with a spa and golf simulator, but the bar, flanked by a duo of climate-controlled wine and spirits cellars is the focal point. Local designer Robert Brown, in collaboration with Kingdom Millworks for construction and cabinet designer Studio Entourage, opted for a dark grasscloth wallcovering paired with high-gloss trim, custom millwork, and steel doors.”Brass and marble accents add a luxurious touch, while warm-stained oak racking and limestone flooring bring warmth and balance to the space,” explains Brown. “The combination of textures, materials, and contrasting finishes creates a sophisticated backdrop that allows the artwork to take center stage.”

A Solar-Powered Hangout Spot

Chicago, Illinois

When local architect Matt Nardella, co-founder of Moss Design, revamped his Chicago basement, he craved a transparent, glass-fronted cellar that invited everyday hangouts. “This isn’t a space I just run down to in order to grab a bottle,” he says. “The cellar has become the place where we listen to music, entertain friends, and let the evening unfold.” Moss’s choice of materials—walnut, steel, polished concrete, and travertine—in the solar-powered cellar are intentionally beautiful in their raw state, and carry evidence of their roots, much like wine. The same two slabs of travertine were used to craft a countertop, backsplash, and custom tasting table, “allowing the material to move elegantly from architecture to furniture,” adds Nardella. 

A Nostalgic Study for World-Class Wine

Highland Park, Texas

Following the remodel of a Highland Park house, the first thing one notices when heading downstairs is the cellar. It’s en route to the cinema beyond, so Naina Hotchkiss and Allison McAfee, partners and principal designers of Dallas-based Park Interiors, wanted it to feel like a transition into something relaxed, “somewhere that slows you down rather than a space you simply pass through. We leaned into a moody, confident palette and treated it almost like a study or trophy room that happened to house exceptional wine,” explains Hotchkiss. Velvety green plaster walls play with bespoke, brass-accented white oak cabinetry, and an antique Persian rug and framed tennis rackets infuse the space with an air of nostalgia. “The way every object was chosen and placed, down to the smallest detail tells you everything about who lives here, their passions, their wins, and their sense of humor about displaying it all so unapologetically,” says McAfee.
